paras: The Vicksburg bulldog lynching was the killing of an unnamed Black man by a white mob in Vicksburg, Mississippi, in late June 1919, after he was accused of intimacy with a white woman. According to the Chicago Whip, the mob buried him to the neck, set a bulldog maddened with red pepper on his head inside an iron cage, and forced prominent Black residents to watch. The Whip, the only paper found with a full account, presented the killing as a crime that the white press had suppressed.

The Whip reported that the man was accused of intimacy with a white woman, adding that "No overt acts of immorality were established" and that only suspected intimacy made up his offense. It gave no name for him and mentioned no arrest or jailing before the mob acted.

In the Whip's account, a mob of "over five hundred" seized the man and took him to a vacant lot. There he was stood in a dugout with only his head above ground and dirt was packed firmly around him. A bulldog's head was covered with a gunny sack of red pepper until the animal was frenzied, and the dog was then placed in an iron cage about five feet square set over the man's head.

The Whip described the dog gouging out the man's eyes and tearing away part of his face and scalp, after which his tongue was pulled from his head and "the natural life of the victim was then taken." Men, women and children were said to have watched; the Whip wrote that women sang, while the Afro-American's shorter version said the crowd "laughed and cheered." The Whip also reported that the most prominent Black people in the area were rounded up, driven to the scene at revolver point, and threatened with the same fate if they published what they had seen.

A Whip dispatch from Vicksburg dated July 7 said Black residents had organized to force a state investigation that would find and arrest "every man connected with the crime." The group, headed by educated young men, wrote to every state official that Black residents were producers and property owners and would act to protect themselves if the state did not. No report of an inquest, arrest or state inquiry appears in the coverage, and the victim's name was never given.

The Chicago Whip broke the story on its front page on July 3 under a headline saying newspapers had "Muzzled" the crime, calling it one of the most "barbarous, fiendish, inhuman murders" and likening the mob to Nero and Attila the Hun. Citing a Whip representative, the paper said the white press had suppressed the killing and that only the New York Evening Post had published it. Its follow-up of July 9 called it "last week's horrible lynching" and described the mob as "the modern Klu Klux."

On July 11 the Baltimore Afro-American printed a short version credited to the Whip, noting that "the daily press as well as associated press carried no word of the outrage." That version differed in small details, giving the charge as intimacy with "a white man" and saying the right eye was gouged first. Earlier, the Cleveland Advocate and Cleveland Gazette of July 5 reported that NAACP assistant secretary Walter F. White had told the association's Cleveland rally of the torture of a Black man in a small Mississippi city two weeks before, an incident he said had been suppressed; neither paper named the city.

The timing is uncertain: the Whip placed the killing "last week" before July 3, while the Afro-American said only "recently." If Walter White's unnamed Mississippi case was the same event, his "two weeks ago" would put it in mid-June instead.

reader.title: Vicksburg bulldog lynching
bases: The Chicago Whip reported that a mob of over five hundred seized a Black man accused of intimacy with a white woman, buried him to the neck and set a bulldog on his head until he died (A6, A7, A9).

The Whip says the victim's 'natural life' was taken by a mob of over five hundred acting with no legal authority, on a suspicion of intimacy with a white woman (A6, A7); all details rest on this one paper's account (A14 is a condensed Whip version).

Every detail comes from the Chicago Whip (A6, A7, A9, A12), and the Afro-American credits its version to the Whip (A14); the NAACP rally report of a suppressed Mississippi torture (A10, A11) does not name the city, so it cannot be counted as independent confirmation.

accounts.label: Chicago Whip (citing a Whip representative)
accounts.gist: A mob of over five hundred seized the man, buried him to the neck, caged a red-pepper-maddened bulldog over his head until it mutilated and killed him, and forced Black citizens to watch.

accounts.label: Baltimore Afro-American (condensed from the Whip)
accounts.gist: Same story in brief, with a man 'charged with intimacy with a white man', the right eye gouged first, and spectators who 'laughed and cheered'.

accounts.label: NAACP speaker Walter F. White
accounts.gist: Told of a suppressed torture of a Black man in an unnamed small Mississippi city two weeks earlier, reported to the conference by a Mississippi delegate.

framing.detail: The Whip called it one of the most 'barbarous, fiendish, inhuman murders', compared the mob to Nero and Attila, and headlined that newspapers had 'Muzzled' the crime.
The Whip's follow-up called it 'last week's horrible lynching' and the mob 'the modern Klu Klux', reporting Black organizing for a state investigation.
The Afro-American headlined 'Vicksburg Mob Tukes Horrible Method of Lynching Man' and stressed the silence of the daily press and AP.
